questions.stem: She ____ in this office for five years.
questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous — for actions started in the past and continuing into the present. 'for five years' / 'since 2019' are the cue phrases. 'Has been working' is the correct form.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: By the time you arrive tomorrow, I ____ the report.
questions.explanation: FUTURE PERFECT — for an action that will be completed BEFORE a specified future time. 'By the time X' takes 'will have + past participle'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: If I ____ more time, I would have helped you.
questions.explanation: Third conditional (past unreal): 'If + past perfect, would have + past participle'. 'had had' = past perfect of 'to have'. Expresses an impossible past condition ('I didn't have time, so I didn't help').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sun ____ in the east.
questions.explanation: Universal truths / habitual facts take SIMPLE PRESENT — 'rises'. The continuous 'is rising' would only be used if describing the specific act right now (e.g., 'Look, the sun is rising').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: When I reached the station, the train ____.
questions.explanation: PAST PERFECT — 'had left' — for an action that was completed BEFORE another past action. 'I reached' (simple past) + 'the train had left' (past perfect — prior to 'reached'). Classic sequence-of-tenses trap.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: This time tomorrow, we ____ on the flight to Paris.
questions.explanation: FUTURE CONTINUOUS — 'will be + -ing' — for actions that will be IN PROGRESS at a specific future time. 'This time tomorrow / next week / at 5pm' are the cue phrases.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: She ____ a letter when the phone rang.
questions.explanation: PAST CONTINUOUS — 'was writing' — for an ongoing past action interrupted by another (simple past) event. 'When the phone rang' is the interrupting event.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses the Past Perfect tense?

options.option_text: I finished my homework before I had gone out to play
I have finished my homework before I went out to play
I had finished my homework before I went out to play
I was finishing my homework before I went out to play

questions.explanation: C is correct: Past Perfect ('had finished') marks the earlier of two past actions — finishing homework came first, then going out. A incorrectly places Past Perfect on the later action ('had gone'), reversing the logical sequence. B uses Present Perfect, which cannot combine coherently with a simple-past reference point. D uses Past Continuous, which signals an ongoing action rather than a completed one.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that correctly uses the Present Perfect Continuous tense.

options.option_text: He is preparing for the competitive exam since January
He has been preparing for the competitive exam since January
He was preparing for the competitive exam since January
He prepares for the competitive exam since January

questions.explanation: B is correct: Present Perfect Continuous ('has been preparing') pairs with 'since' to show an action that began at a past point and is still ongoing. A (Present Continuous) and C (Past Continuous) cannot correctly combine with 'since' for duration-from-a-past-moment. D (Simple Present) expresses habit or universal truth, not a span of time anchored to a past date.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'When he retires next year, he ____ for the civil services for nearly four decades'.

options.option_text: will be working as a senior official
has been working as a senior official
would have been working as a senior official
will have been working as a senior official

questions.explanation: D is correct: Future Perfect Continuous ('will have been working') expresses a prolonged action still in progress at a defined future point, stressing its total duration. A (Future Continuous) signals an ongoing future action without the emphasis on accumulated duration. B (Present Perfect Continuous) is grammatically inconsistent with the future time-marker 'next year'. C uses the conditional 'would', which requires a stated condition — none exists here.

questions.stem: Identify the sentence with an INCORRECT use of inverted tense structure.

options.option_text: No sooner had the match started than it began to pour heavily
No sooner did the bell ring than the students rush out of class
Scarcely had he entered the building when the alarm went off
Hardly had the chief guest arrived when the function commenced

questions.explanation: B is incorrect: the structure 'No sooner did + subject + base verb + than + subject + V2' requires the result clause to use Simple Past; 'rush' (base form) must be 'rushed'. A, C, and D correctly follow the inverted Past Perfect pattern — 'No sooner/Scarcely/Hardly + had + subject + V3 + than/when + subject + Simple Past'. This is a high-frequency SSC/IBPS inversion trap.

questions.stem: The manager said, 'My team is working on the new project.' Which reported speech form is CORRECT?

options.option_text: The manager said that his team was working on the new project
The manager said that his team is working on the new project
The manager told that his team was working on the new project
The manager said that his team had been working on the new project

questions.explanation: A is correct: Present Continuous ('is working') backshifts to Past Continuous ('was working') in reported speech. B retains the original tense — a classic backshift error. C uses 'told that' without an indirect object; 'tell' always needs one ('told us that'), making C ungrammatical. D over-backshifts to Past Perfect Continuous, which is reserved for cases where the original verb was itself already in the past.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly expresses a mixed conditional, where a past condition produces a present-state consequence?

options.option_text: If he had invested wisely, he would have been wealthy by now
If he invested wisely, he would be wealthy and financially secure
If he had invested wisely, he would be wealthy and financially secure now
If he invests wisely, he will become wealthy and financially secure

questions.explanation: C is correct: the mixed conditional uses 'If + Past Perfect' (unfulfilled past condition) with 'would + base verb' (present-state result). A is a pure Third Conditional — both condition and result are past ('would have been'). B is a Second Conditional — a present hypothetical with no link to an unrealised past action. D is a First Conditional — a real and achievable future scenario, not a counterfactual at all.

questions.stem: Fill in the blanks: 'Investigators confirmed that the building ____ for decades before the authorities finally ____ it down'.
questions.explanation: A is correct: 'had been deteriorating' (Past Perfect Continuous) shows a prolonged action still ongoing at the moment the later event occurred; 'brought' (Simple Past) correctly marks that subsequent completed event. B reverses the temporal logic — Past Perfect belongs to the earlier action, not to 'bringing down'. C uses Present Perfect Continuous, incompatible with the past-narrative frame established by 'confirmed'. D mixes Past Perfect Continuous with Present Perfect ('have brought'), creating an incoherent tense sequence within a single past-time clause.

questions.stem: The delegates ____ in the conference hall for over an hour before the chief guest arrived.
questions.explanation: C is correct because the waiting started and continued before another past event (the guest arriving), which requires the past perfect continuous 'had been waiting'. Option B ('have been waiting') is wrong because present perfect cannot be used for an action completed before a past reference point. Option A ('were waiting') misses the 'before' relationship and describes simultaneous action, not prior duration.

questions.stem: Neither the manager nor the employees ____ anything about the sudden policy change announced yesterday.

options.option_text: had been knowing about it then

questions.explanation: C is correct because 'yesterday' anchors the event to a completed past time, requiring simple past 'knew'. 'Know' is a stative verb and must never be used in continuous forms — so Options A ('were knowing') and D ('had been knowing') are grammatically wrong. Option B ('have known') fails because present perfect cannot co-occur with a specific past time marker like 'yesterday'.

questions.stem: By the time the auditors submit their report next month, the accounts department ____ all the discrepancies.

options.option_text: would have rectified most of them

questions.explanation: A is correct because 'By the time + present simple (submit)' in a future context requires future perfect ('will have rectified') in the main clause, showing completion before a future deadline. Option C ('will be rectifying') indicates an ongoing future action, not completion. Option B uses 'would have', which belongs to hypothetical conditionals, not factual future sequences. Option D uses present perfect, which cannot refer to a future action.

questions.stem: The government ____ several infrastructure projects in the northeastern states since 2019.
questions.explanation: B is correct because 'since 2019' signals a period from a past point up to now, requiring present perfect ('has launched') to show ongoing relevance to the present. Option A (simple past 'launched') is the most tempting distractor but ignores the present-relevance signalled by 'since'. Option C (past perfect 'had launched') implies a prior-past context that is absent here. Option D (past continuous) cannot link with 'since' in standard grammar.

questions.stem: If she ____ the application form correctly, her candidature would not have been rejected.

options.option_text: had filled in the form correctly
was filling in that online form

questions.explanation: C is correct because the result clause 'would not have been rejected' (would have + V3) identifies this as a Type 3 (unreal past) conditional, which demands 'had + V3' in the if-clause. Option B ('took') signals a Type 2 conditional whose result clause would be 'would not be', not 'would not have been' — mixing the two types is the classic error. Option D ('was filling') is a past continuous and does not fit any standard conditional pattern here.

questions.stem: The magistrate observed that the accused ____ in the town on the night the robbery ____.

options.option_text: had been present / had taken place

questions.explanation: B is correct because in reported speech, 'observed' (reporting verb in past) triggers backshift: simple past → past perfect, and simple past in the subordinate time clause also shifts to past perfect ('had taken place'). Option A ('was present / has taken place') fails because 'has taken place' is present perfect and cannot survive backshift into reported past speech. Option D ('has been present / took place') mixes present perfect and simple past — neither is appropriately backshifted.

questions.stem: Scarcely ____ the board meeting when the CEO ____ everyone with the acquisition announcement.
questions.explanation: C is correct because 'Scarcely...when' is a correlative adverb of negative inversion requiring past perfect in the first clause ('had begun') and simple past in the 'when' clause ('surprised'). This mirrors the 'Hardly/No sooner...than' pattern tested frequently in SSC. Option B ('started / surprised') uses simple past for both clauses, missing the mandatory inversion with past perfect. Option A is wrong because 'has surprised' is present perfect — both clauses must be in the past for this construction.
